opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so scalable oversight was really the starting point for me. The basic worry is this: right now we supervise AI systems by checking their outputs. We label data, we rate responses, we tell the model when it's right or wrong. That works fine as long as we're actually able to tell. But if these systems keep getting more capable, we'll eventually be asking them questions where we can't easily verify the answers ourselves. That could be novel science, complicated code, long-horizon reasoning. And then the question becomes: how do you supervise something that knows more than you do in a given domain?

There were a bunch of proposed approaches to this, like debate, where two models argue and a weaker judge decides, and various kinds of assisted evaluation. But when we wanted to actually test these ideas empirically, we kept hitting the same problem. You need a testbed where there's a real gap between the system and the overseer. And you need ground truth that you, the experimenter, can trust, even though the overseer in the experiment can't easily get to it.

That's really what GPQA came out of. The idea was to build questions that are genuinely hard, written by people with or pursuing PhDs in biology, physics, and chemistry, where other experts in that field can mostly get them right, but highly skilled people from *outside* that field can't. And that holds even when they have unrestricted web access and spend a long time on each question, often half an hour or more. That's the "Google-proof" part. If you can just search for the answer, it doesn't give you an oversight gap. The non-experts landed only modestly above chance, while the domain experts did substantially better. That gap is exactly the thing we wanted to study.

So the hope was that you could use it as a sandbox. Take non-expert humans, or weaker models, as the overseers. Take a stronger model, or an expert, as the thing being overseen. Then ask whether your oversight protocol helps the weak overseer reach the right answer reliably, and crucially, whether it keeps them from being persuaded of wrong answers.

What happened, of course, is that people mostly started using it as a straight capabilities benchmark. That's fine, and honestly kind of interesting in its own right, because it showed how quickly frontier models went from mediocre to expert-level on it. But it also says something about evaluations generally. Benchmarks saturate fast now, and the deeper question of how we verify answers we can't check ourselves doesn't go away just because a model gets a high score. If anything, it gets more pressing.

r001.rationale: The response says scalable oversight addresses how to supervise systems when people cannot easily verify their answers, and describes testing whether oversight helps a weaker overseer reach correct answers reliably.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I got into this was really through the scalable oversight framing, which is the question: how do we supervise models that are becoming more capable than the people who are supposed to be checking them? The classic setup for training and evaluating these systems assumes you have some human who can look at the output and say whether it's right. And that assumption starts to break down once the model knows more than the human about the domain.

What struck me is that the problem isn't just a training problem, it's an evaluation problem too. If I want to study scalable oversight empirically, I need a setting where a non-expert genuinely can't verify the answer on their own, but where there's still some ground truth that an expert can confirm. Otherwise you can't tell whether your oversight method is working or whether the overseer is just getting fooled.

And when we looked at the existing benchmarks, almost none of them had that property. Things like MMLU are hard-ish, but a motivated person with internet access can usually look up the answer in a few minutes. So you can't use them to simulate the regime we actually care about, where the human is really out of their depth.

That was the motivation for GPQA. We wanted questions written by people with PhDs or in PhD programs in biology, physics, chemistry, where other experts in the same subfield would get them right, but skilled non-experts with unrestricted web access, spending something like half an hour per question, would still mostly fail. We ended up with experts around 65 percent, or closer to 74 if you account for the mistakes they later identified, and the non-experts around 34 percent even with all that effort. That gap is the whole point. It's a sandbox for asking: can a non-expert, with help from a model, or from a debate between models, reliably figure out the truth on a question they couldn't crack on their own?

The other thing it does is give you a frontier capability measure that isn't contaminated by "could you just Google this." At the time GPT-4 was around 39 percent, which was close to the non-expert baseline. So it served both purposes: tracking how far models are from expert performance, and giving us a realistic testbed for oversight methods before the stakes get too high to experiment.

r001.rationale: The response frames scalable oversight as supervising models that exceed human expertise and evaluating whether a non-expert can reliably determine the truth with help, despite being unable to verify the answer alone.

astra-6.text:
The core question for me was: how do we supervise an AI system when it can do things that we can’t easily judge? With current systems, we often evaluate an answer by having a person look at it and say whether it’s right. But as systems become more capable, that person may not have the expertise needed to tell. And being persuasive isn’t the same thing as being correct.

That motivated GPQA. We wanted a setting where answering the questions requires real expertise, and where a non-expert can’t just look up the answer—even with access to the internet and a substantial amount of time. So we used difficult questions written by experts in biology, chemistry, and physics, and checked how well other experts and non-experts could answer them.

The connection to scalable oversight is that this gives you a way to study an expertise gap. Could an AI help a non-expert reliably judge an answer to one of these questions? What kind of explanation or interaction would actually help them distinguish a correct answer from a convincing wrong one? We still have experts who can check the result, so we can test whether an oversight method works before we’re in a situation where no human can independently assess what the model is doing. GPQA doesn’t solve that problem, but it gives us a concrete setting in which to start studying it.

r001.rationale: The response frames scalable oversight as helping non-experts reliably judge whether AI answers are correct when they lack the relevant expertise, which communicates establishing confidence in model outputs under that expertise gap.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem with scalable oversight is: how do you supervise a system when it can do things that you can’t reliably evaluate yourself? If a model gives you an answer to a difficult scientific question, and you don’t know the subject, how do you tell whether it’s correct or just sounds convincing?

That motivated GPQA as a setting where we could study that gap. We wanted questions that experts could answer, but that were difficult for non-experts even with access to the internet. The point wasn’t just to make a harder benchmark. It was to have problems where we could establish the correct answer through expert judgment, and then ask whether some oversight procedure could help a less knowledgeable person evaluate a model’s answer.

So you can think of it as a testbed for scalable oversight: can we use AI assistance to help people judge work that would otherwise be beyond their expertise? A model’s score is useful, but the bigger question is whether our ability to supervise these systems can keep up with their capabilities.

r001.rationale: It describes supervising a model when evaluators cannot reliably assess its answers themselves, and explains using expert judgment to establish correctness.
